question: Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease characterised by high blood glucose levels as a result of insufficient insulin production or an altered response to the hormone. It manifests as type 1 (T1D), which is autoimmune in origin, or type 2 (T2D), which is more common and linked to genetic and lifestyle factors.

T1D requires daily management supported by advanced technological devices such as continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems, insulin infusion pumps, and digital platforms for therapeutic follow-up. While T2D can often be managed with diet and non‑insulin medications, it can also benefit from the use of CGM systems.

Current EU legislation does not establish minimum quality requirements for these devices, allowing products with variable safety and efficacy standards to enter the market. This results in a dual risk: possible compromise of patients’ clinical safety and market distortion in favour of less effective but cheaper products. In the light of this: 1.

Does the Commission intend to define binding minimum standards, based on scientific evidence, for diabetes management medical devices, including the possibility of modelling quality standards such as but not limited to those identified by the US Food and Drug Administration (iCGM)?
How does it plan to ensure a coordinated assessment of the quality and clinical effectiveness of such devices within the single market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.3.2026) Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices1 and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices2 lay down general safety and performance requirements to ensure a high level of protection of health and safety of patients and users while supporting innovation. Such requirements are implemented via the corresponding conformity assessment procedures.

Technical specifications in support of those requirements are usually laid down in harmonised standards. Devices designed and manufactured in compliance with harmonised standards benefit from a presumption of conformity with the corresponding requirements of the applicable legislation. However, those requirements are applicable in all Member States regardless of the existence of standards.

Harmonised standards are available on quality management systems3 and risk management4 for blood-glucose monitoring systems5 and for infusion pumps and controllers6, among others. Other harmonised standards are being developed or revised by the relevant European standardisation organisations, CEN and CENELEC7, upon a request from the Commission8.

Where no harmonised standards exist, where relevant standards are not sufficient, or where there is a need to address public health concerns, the Commission may adopt common specifications in respect of the requirements set out in the abovementioned Regulations.

The responsibility on the quality, safety and effectiveness of medical devices on the EU market lies with the competent authorities of the Member States in charge of the enforcement of the EU rules on medical devices and the related market surveillance activities. The Commission ensures coordination at EU level through the Medical Device Coordination Group (MDCG).
1 Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on medical devices,

amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and repealing Council Directives 90/385/EEC and 93/42/EEC (OJ L 117, 5.5.2017, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/745/oj).

2 Regulation (EU) 2017/746 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices and repealing Directive 98/79/EC and Commission Decision 2010/227/EU (OJ L 117, 5.5.2017, p. 176, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/746/oj). 3 EN ISO 13485:2016 + AC:2008 + A11:2021 Medical devices - Quality management systems - Requirements for regulatory purposes.

4 EN ISO 14971:2019 + A11:2021 Medical devices - Application of risk management to medical devices. 5 EN ISO 15197:2015 In vitro diagnostic test systems - Requirements for blood-glucose monitoring systems for self-testing in managing diabetes mellitus. 6 IEC 60601-2-24 Medical electrical equipment - Part 2-24: Particular requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of infusion pumps and controllers.

7 The European Committee for Standardization (CEN) and the European Electrotechnical Committee for Standardization (CENELEC): https://www.cencenelec.eu/european-standardization/cen-and-cenelec/. 8 Commission Implementing Decision of 14.4.
